nameStory: Field woodrush gets its name from its preference for open fields and meadows, distinguishing it from woodland rushes. It's also charmingly called 'Good Friday grass' in some regions because it often begins flowering around Easter time in early spring.
description: Field woodrush is a small, clumping grass-like plant that forms neat tufts about 4-12 inches tall. Despite its grassy appearance, it's actually in the rush family, not the grass family. The plant produces distinctive clusters of small, brownish flowers that look like tiny brushes or brooms perched atop slender stems. Its narrow leaves are soft and somewhat hairy, quite different from the stiff, smooth leaves of true grasses.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small brownish flower clusters that look like miniature bottle brushes or chimney sweeps, giving the plant its nickname 'sweep's broom'

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, with fine hairs along the edges that catch morning dew

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small, neat clumps or tufts rather than spreading extensively, typically 4-12 inches tall

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, wiry stems that feel firm but flexible when gently bent between your fingers

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, glossy brown seeds with a small white cap that looks like a miniature chef's hat

habitat: Field woodrush thrives in open, sunny locations including meadows, fields, lawns, and disturbed grasslands throughout New England. It prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate both acidic and neutral conditions. You'll often find it mixed in with other low-growing plants in areas that get regular sunlight.

seasonality.spring: Flowering begins in early spring, often around April, with the distinctive brush-like flower clusters appearing on fresh green stems.
seasonality.summer: Seeds ripen and the plant maintains its tufted appearance, though flowers fade to brown. Leaves remain green and soft.
seasonality.fall: Plant begins to go dormant, with leaves turning yellowish-brown but often persisting through early winter.
seasonality.winter: Dried leaves and stems may remain visible above snow, appearing as small brown tufts in the landscape.

funFact: This innocent-looking little plant is actually a master of deception — it looks so much like grass that it regularly sneaks into carefully manicured lawns and golf course greens, where groundskeepers often mistake it for a desirable turf grass until those telltale brush-like flowers give it away!
confusionNotes: Field woodrush is most commonly confused with young grass clumps, but the hairy leaf edges and distinctive brush-like flowers are dead giveaways. Remember: if it has fuzzy leaves and looks like tiny bottle brushes are growing out of it, it's a woodrush, not grass!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'woodrush,' this species actually prefers open fields rather than woods, which can confuse beginners. The 'rush' part of the name refers to its family relationship to true rushes, though woodrushes have softer, hairier leaves compared to their smooth-leaved rush cousins.
compareHints: Field woodrush is the most common and widespread woodrush in New England, distinguished from its relatives by its preference for open, sunny habitats rather than shady woods. Compared to heath wood-rush, it forms smaller, neater clumps and has less branched flower clusters. Unlike hairy woodrush, which prefers forests, field woodrush thrives in disturbed and cultivated areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Heath wood-rush differs from field woodrush by having flower clusters on variable-length stalks rather than in tight, rounded heads.

Hairy woodrush is distinguished from other New England woodrushes primarily by its prominent white hairs along the leaf edges - field woodrush has much less noticeable hairs, while heath woodrush tends to grow in more open, acidic areas.
Unlike other New England woodrushes that grow in lower elevation forests and fields, spiked woodrush is the high-altitude specialist of the group.
Small-flower woodrush lives up to its name with much smaller, less noticeable flowers than other New England woodrushes.
**[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Bulbous woodrush stands apart from other New England woodrushes primarily by its distinctive bulbous base structures, which other species lack.
White woodrush differs from other New England woodrushes by its whitish flowers (rather than brown or reddish) and preference for oak forests specifically.
